newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SMH sees no danger of hostile takeover.
newsitem.headline: SMH sees no danger of hostile takeover.

text.p: Swiss watchmaker Ste Suisse Microelectronique et d'Horlogerie SA (SMH) is positioned to fend off any hostile takeover bid despite some shareholders' departure from the so-called "Hayek pool", officials said.

Company President Nicolas Hayek told Reuters at the company's annual meeting that he personally owned 30 percent of SMH voting rights. He and other shareholders still in the pool controlled just over 40 percent of the votes, he added.
He also won shareholder approval to raise to 49 percent from 33-1/3 percent the ceiling at which a shareholder or group has to make an offer to acquire all the shares.
This allows Hayek and his allies to stock up their stakes to just under the 49 percent level.

SMH or its units hold "seven to eight" percent of the company's own shares, but these are not entitled to votes, so the current stakes by Hayek and his allies "are enough to control the company because practically only 92 to 93 percent of all shares now have voting rights", he said.
In addition, all the company's shareholders would not attend an annual meeting, Hayek noted. Owners representing 75 percent of the voting rights were represented at today's meeting.
Shareholders also agreed to drop the current statute limiting foreigners' stakes to 30 percent of total capital, and to raise the voting rights limit to five percent from three.
One company official said this would make SMH more attractive to foreign investors.

The pool agreement -- first struck in 1985 and extended in 1992 -- expires on June 30, but allows members to decide whether to remain or not as of 1997. Some investors, including Stephan Schmidheiny, have already sold or reduced their stakes.
